name: Comply with Ontario's distribution safety regulation (Regulation 22/04)
summary: Ontario Regulation 22/04 makes every licensed distributor report serious electrical incidents to the Electrical Safety Authority (ESA) within 48 hours, answer ESA's due diligence inspections and public safety concerns, and pass an annual audit and declaration of compliance. At a city-owned distributor a safety advisor runs these items: reporting contacts by contractors and homeowners with utility lines, getting field supervisors to verify and repair hazards that ESA finds, and assembling evidence with the standards engineer for the annual audit. The work is slow because ESA reviews and field repairs take weeks, and the audit evidence sits in many record systems.

baseline.org_archetype: A municipally owned Ontario electricity distributor of about 570 staff and 346,000 customers that reported 20 public contacts and no serious incidents to ESA in 2021 and was rated compliant.
baseline.notes: Items are tracked in a compliance spreadsheet and the health and safety incident system; ESA correspondence is by email. ESA's online incident form started in August 2022, so phone and email reporting is the reference practice.

unit_of_work: one ESA reportable item (incident report, ESA finding or concern, or the annual audit and declaration)
trigger: A contact with utility plant is reported, ESA sends a due diligence inspection finding or public safety concern, an inspector finds a public hazard, or ESA's bulletin opens the annual audit.
end_state: The item is reported and accepted or answered, ESA has closed it, and the compliance register and scorecard data are updated.

volume.seasonality: Public contacts peak from May to October with construction, pool installation and tree work near lines; the annual audit and declaration fall in the months after the group's audit period ends; scorecard data checks fall in March and April.

evidence.note: 20 public incidents reported to ESA in 2021 (ho_sc2021), about 1.7 a month; about 12 ESA findings and concerns and one audit cycle a year are the author's estimate, giving about 3 items a month.

surge.cause: major storm with many downed lines

evidence.note: Organisation file assumption of one to four major events a year. Downed lines near the public raise reports, though contacts caused by weather that is force majeure need not be reported (esa_seir); the multiplier is the author's estimate.

Organisation file role (6). One advisor acts as the distribution safety compliance lead; about 0.2 FTE goes to ESA reportable items, findings and the annual audit evidence. Public awareness campaigns are outside this workflow.
Organisation file role (1). Decides reportability, signs ESA responses and runs the annual audit engagement.

Organisation file role (3, professional engineers). Holds the approval records for equipment, designs and the construction verification program that the annual audit samples, and reviews items that point to a standard.
Organisation file role (8). Verifies ESA findings in the field and arranges the corrective work. Not listed for this process in the organisation file's process map.

roles.title: Vice-President (operations, engineering, customer service, finance, corporate services)
roles.department: Office of the President and CEO

evidence.note: Organisation file role (5). An officer signs the annual Declaration of Compliance (esa_decl allows a professional engineer, director or officer); the vice-president of operations is assumed. Not listed for this process in the organisation file's process map.

systems.name: Health, safety and environment incident system
Ontario One Call member portal and locate management
Geographic information system (asset and network model)
Document management and engineering drawing repository
ERP: general ledger, work orders, purchasing, inventory, fixed assets
Mobile workforce management and field tablets

resources.name: Light vehicle (pickup or van) for locators, meter technicians, inspectors and field service

steps.name: Receive the item and open a compliance record
steps.description: The distribution safety compliance advisor receives the item: an incident report from the control room or a crew about a member of the public or a contractor contacting utility plant, a letter or email from an ESA inspector about a due diligence inspection or a public safety concern, an inspection finding of a public hazard, or ESA's annual audit notice. They open a record in the compliance tracker with the date and time the utility became aware.

error.defect_description: Awareness time recorded late, so the 48-hour clock looks met when it was not.

evidence.note: Item types from the five Component B elements (oeb_psguide) and section 12 reporting (esa_seir). The awareness time matters because the 48-hour clock starts when the utility realises an incident is serious (esa_seir).

steps.name: Classify the item
steps.description: The advisor decides what kind of item it is: a contact or fire involving the public or a contractor, an ESA finding or public safety concern that needs a field fix and a reply, or the annual audit and declaration cycle.

next.condition: public or contractor contact, fire or explosion
ESA finding, public safety concern or inspection hazard

evidence.note: 20 public incidents reported in 2021 (ho_sc2021) give about 1.7 a month, about 60 percent of the organisation file's 3 items a month; ESA findings and public safety concerns (about 12 a year) and one audit cycle a year are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Gather the facts of the contact
steps.description: The advisor pulls the outage or trouble record, the crew's make-safe notes and photos, and for dig-ins the locate ticket from the One Call portal, and calls the crew lead or the control room operator to confirm what was hit, the voltage and whether anyone was hurt.

error.defect_description: Voltage or locate status recorded wrongly.

evidence.note: The facts gathered follow the ESA reporting form (location, voltage, locates requested and accurate, excavation inside the locate area, weather, injury). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Decide whether the incident is a mandatory report
steps.description: The safety manager compares the facts with the serious electrical incident definition: death or critical injury, or contact, fire or explosion at 750 volts or above with the potential for death or critical injury, and not caused by force majeure. When unsure, the guideline says to report first and settle the class with ESA afterwards.

error.defect_description: A reportable incident is treated as voluntary and reported late.

control.basis: Ontario Regulation 22/04 s. 12: serious electrical incident definition

evidence.note: Definition, force majeure exception, report-first advice and voluntary reporting from the ESA guideline.

steps.name: Report the incident to ESA
steps.description: The advisor fills in the ESA serious electrical incident reporting form (caller, location, date and time of incident and of awareness, other authorities involved, nature of incident, site information and a description with photos) and sends it by email, or phones the ESA line, within 48 hours. Contacts that are not mandatory are sent as voluntary reports.

control.basis: Ontario Regulation 22/04 s. 12: report serious electrical incidents to ESA within 48 hours of becoming aware

evidence.note: 48-hour deadline and form content from esa_seir; the utility reported all 20 public contacts in 2021 though none was serious (ho_sc2021).

steps.name: Drive to the contact site
steps.description: The advisor drives a light vehicle to the site, usually after the crew has made it safe, to see the clearances, the barrier or enclosure damage, the excavation or the equipment that touched the line.

evidence.note: Travel time across a 1,116 square kilometre territory and the one-day typical delay are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Document site conditions
steps.description: The advisor photographs and measures the site: overhead clearance to the building, sign or equipment, depth and location of the cable against the locate marks, and whether the plant met the utility's construction standard. They note any public hazard that still needs a fix.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of the site review that supports the ESA file and a possible damage recovery claim.

steps.name: Wait for ESA's review of the report
steps.description: ESA's powerlines staff review the report, decide whether it counts as a mandatory serious incident for the scorecard or a voluntary report, and may contact the utility for more information or assistance.

evidence.note: ESA may contact the distributor for information and the distributor must assist on request (s. 12(3.1)). Review time and the share of follow-up requests are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Answer ESA's information request
steps.description: The advisor writes a reply with the site notes, photos, locate records and crew statements that ESA asked for, and the safety manager reviews it before it is sent.

control.basis: Ontario Regulation 22/04 s. 12(3.1): assist ESA investigations on request

evidence.note: Duty to assist from s. 12(3.1); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Write to the contractor about safe limits of approach
steps.description: For a contractor or homeowner contact the advisor sends a letter or arranges a visit to the firm about limits of approach to overhead lines or calling for locates, and passes damage details to the claims specialist for cost recovery.

evidence.note: The utility's safety partners made 32 site visits to third-party contractors on limits of approach in 2021 (ho_sc2021). Times and the standards referral share are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Log the ESA finding and assign an owner
steps.description: The advisor logs the ESA due diligence inspection finding, public safety concern or inspection-found hazard (for example a damaged pad-mount transformer enclosure, a low conductor, or a missing guard), looks up the asset in GIS and assigns it to the area supervisor with ESA's reply date.

error.defect_description: Asset identified wrongly from the inspector's description.

evidence.note: Due diligence inspections and public safety concerns are Component B elements (oeb_psguide) that the utility answered in 2021 (ho_sc2021); examples and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Drive to the reported location
steps.description: The area supervisor drives a light vehicle to the asset named in the finding, usually fitting the visit in on the way between crew sites, so it can wait a few days.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Verify the condition and arrange a temporary fix
steps.description: The supervisor checks the condition against the construction standard, photographs it, has it made safe on the spot if there is exposure to the public (a lock, barricade or call-out of the trouble truck), and raises a maintenance work order for the permanent repair.

control.basis: Company public safety procedure: make public hazards safe on discovery

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the repair itself is done in the maintenance and construction processes.

steps.name: Follow the repair until it is done
steps.description: The supervisor tracks the work order through scheduling, chases the planner when a crew or material is not available, and collects the completion photos when the crew finishes.

evidence.note: Repair waits of three days to a month for crew time and material are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Draft the response to ESA
steps.description: The advisor writes the response to the inspector: what was found, the temporary and permanent fixes with dates and photos, and any change to the inspection or construction practice to stop it recurring.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve and send the ESA response
steps.description: The safety manager reads the response, checks that the photos show the fix and that the dates meet ESA's deadline, then signs it and emails it to the inspector.

control.basis: Ontario Regulation 22/04 compliance follow-up: written response to ESA findings

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for ESA to accept the response
steps.description: ESA's inspector reviews the response and photos and either closes the finding in ESA's records or writes back asking for more repair work or more evidence.

next.condition: ESA asks for more work or evidence
accepted; points to a construction standard

evidence.note: ESA review time and re-work share are the author's estimate; the utility was rated compliant in 2021 (ho_sc2021), so few findings escalate.

steps.name: Engage an ESA-approved auditor
steps.description: After ESA's bulletin sets the audit period and due date for the utility's group, the safety manager confirms the auditor is on ESA's approved list (or gets ESA's approval first), issues the purchase order and agrees the audit plan and dates.

control.basis: Ontario Regulation 22/04 s. 13: annual audit by an ESA-approved auditor

evidence.note: ESA notifies the audit period and due date and must approve the auditor before engagement; twelve-month audit period with the report due three months after it ends.

steps.name: Compile approval and construction verification records
steps.description: The standards engineer assembles the evidence for sections 4 to 8: equipment approvals and test records, P.Eng-certified standard designs, the construction verification program and a sample of inspection certificates for new, like-for-like and emergency work, and the maintenance program records.

evidence.note: Audit scope from esa_audit sections 2.1.1 to 2.1.4; 20 to 80 hours of preparation for a distributor of this size is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Compile incident and declaration evidence
steps.description: In parallel the advisor gathers the section 12 incident reports and ESA replies, the public safety concern and due diligence files, and the evidence for the sections the declaration covers.

evidence.note: Declaration covers sections 3, 9, 10, 11 and 12 (esa_decl); effort is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for the auditor's fieldwork
steps.description: The auditor interviews senior managers on the control environment, works through ESA's checklist and samples plans, test records and installed construction in the field.

evidence.note: Routine audits take 21 to 36 auditor hours, longer for larger distributors (esa_audit); elapsed time of one to two weeks is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Support auditor interviews and field sampling
steps.description: The standards engineer answers the auditor's questions, pulls the extra records the auditor samples and takes the auditor to installed sites to compare the construction with the approved design.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Write the management response and action plan
steps.description: When the auditor reviews the draft findings with the utility, the safety manager writes the management response and an action plan with owners and dates for each Needs Improvement item.

evidence.note: The distributor submits the audit report with a management response and action plan (esa_audit step vii); effort is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Sign the annual Declaration of Compliance
steps.description: The vice-president reads the declaration that the utility is in full compliance with sections 3, 9, 10, 11 and 12, or lists any non-compliance with the action plan, checks the stated methodology and signs it.

control.basis: Ontario Regulation 22/04 s. 14: declaration signed by a professional engineer, director or officer

evidence.note: Signed by a professional engineer or a director or officer and due with the audit report (esa_decl); which officer signs is the author's assumption.

steps.name: Submit the audit report and declaration to ESA
steps.description: The safety manager sends the audit report, management response, action plan and the signed declaration to ESA by the group's due date and files copies for the scorecard.

control.basis: Ontario Regulation 22/04 ss. 13-14: annual audit report and declaration due to ESA

evidence.note: Submission contents and timing from the two guidelines.

steps.name: Wait for ESA's review meeting
steps.description: ESA reviews the report, response and action plan, then meets the utility to agree any actions needed for compliance and the compliance rating that feeds the scorecard.

evidence.note: ESA review and meeting are steps viii and ix of the audit process (esa_audit); the rating feeds Component B (oeb_psguide). Elapsed time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review the construction standard involved
steps.description: The standards engineer checks whether the standard, approved material or clearance rule involved should change, for example a deeper burial depth, a different enclosure lock or a clearance table update, and opens a standards change if so.

evidence.note: Link to standards maintenance is in the organisation file's process map; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Update the compliance register and scorecard data
steps.description: The advisor closes the item in the compliance tracker with its ESA class and outcome, so the year's incident counts and compliance status can be checked against ESA's scorecard data before the April 30 RRR filing.

error.defect_description: Item counted in the wrong reporting year.

evidence.note: ESA sends Component B and C data two months before the April 30 due date and accepts feedback up to a month before (oeb_psguide); per-item effort is the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: ESA asks for more information on an incident
exceptions.description: ESA's review of a contact report raises questions, and the advisor must assemble and send more records before ESA classifies it.

exceptions.name: ESA not satisfied with a finding response
exceptions.description: ESA asks for more repair work or evidence, so the supervisor goes back to the work order and the response is redone.

exceptions.name: No defect found at the reported location
exceptions.description: The supervisor finds the asset already meets the standard, and the response to ESA explains this with photos.

exceptions.name: Standards change after an incident or finding
exceptions.description: The incident or finding shows a standard, material or clearance rule should change, so the standards engineer reviews it before closure.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from receipt to item closed
benchmarks.population: All Regulation 22/04 items at a mid-size Ontario distributor, 2019-2022

evidence.note: No published figure found. Author's estimate: incident reports are sent within 48 hours but ESA review and contractor follow-up take two to four weeks; findings take three to eight weeks for repair and ESA acceptance; the audit cycle takes several months but is rare.

benchmarks.population: Ontario licensed distributors and their contractors

benchmarks.unit: incidents reported to ESA per year (none serious)
serious incidents involving the public per 1,000 km of line
benchmarks.population: Hydro Ottawa Limited 2021 industry target; achieved 0

benchmarks.unit: months after the twelve-month audit period ends
auditor hours for a routine audit
benchmarks.population: Ontario distributors, ESA estimate (larger distributors take longer)

pain_points.description: Classifying a contact as mandatory or voluntary under the 48-hour clock needs facts from the crew, control room and locate records that arrive piecemeal, so many contacts are reported 'just in case' and classified later with ESA.

evidence.note: Report-first advice in esa_seir; 20 contacts reported and none serious in ho_sc2021.

pain_points.description: Repairs for ESA findings compete with planned and storm work for crew time, so responses wait weeks for a work order to be done.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Audit evidence (approvals, P.Eng-certified designs, inspection certificates, maintenance records) sits in document, ERP and GIS systems, and the standards engineer spends days assembling it each year.

evidence.note: Scope from esa_audit; effort is the author's estimate.

pain_points.description: The year's incident counts and compliance status are reconciled by hand against ESA's scorecard data in the weeks before the April 30 filing.

evidence.note: Scorecard data timeline from oeb_psguide.

sources.title: Guideline for Section 12 of Ontario Regulation 22/04: Reporting of Serious Electrical Incidents, Version 4.1.2
sources.supports: Distributors and their contractors must report any serious electrical incident to ESA within 48 hours of becoming aware of it, by telephone, fax or email using the Appendix A form; definition of serious electrical incident (death or critical injury from electrical contact, or inadvertent contact, fire or explosion at 750 V or above or in a meter with the potential for death or critical injury, force majeure excepted); worker-only incidents reported to the Ministry of Labour are exempt; voluntary reporting encouraged and unsure cases should be reported first and classified with ESA afterwards; ESA may ask the distributor for information or assistance (s. 12(3.1)); vegetation, animal contacts, safe equipment failures and customer-owned equipment are not reportable.

sources.title: Guideline for Audit, Version 2.1, Ontario Regulation 22/04 Electrical Distribution Safety
sources.supports: Annual audit of compliance with sections 4 to 8 (equipment approval, P.Eng-certified designs, inspection of all construction before energization, operating and maintenance programs); ESA must approve the auditor before engagement; ten-step audit process (ESA notice, auditor approval, engagement, audit program, fieldwork, report reviewed with distributor, distributor submits report with management response and action plan, ESA review, ESA meeting, progress reports); distributors in three groups, twelve-month audit period, report due three months after the period ends; routine audit effort 21 to 36 auditor hours depending on control environment, longer for larger distributors; records kept at least one year after the audit.

sources.title: Guideline for Declaration of Compliance, Revision 2.1, Ontario Regulation 22/04
sources.supports: Section 14 requires an annual Declaration of Compliance with sections 3, 9, 10, 11 and 12, signed by a professional engineer or a director or officer, due with the annual audit report; it states full compliance or lists non-compliances with an action plan, and names the methodology used (senior management review, independent managers, auditors, compliance officer or other).

sources.title: Electrical Distribution Safety: Public Safety Scorecard Metrics Guide, Components B and C, R2
sources.publisher: Electrical Safety Authority, hosted by the Ontario Energy Board
sources.supports: Component B (compliance with Regulation 22/04) is built from five elements: audit, declaration of compliance, due diligence inspections, public safety concerns and compliance investigations, rated Compliant, Needs Improvement or Non-Compliant; Component C counts serious electrical incidents involving the public per 1,000 km of line; ESA sends scorecard data two months before the April 30 RRR 2.1.19 due date and accepts distributor feedback up to one month before it.

sources.title: Scorecard - Hydro Ottawa Limited (2017-2021) and 2021 Scorecard Management Discussion and Analysis
sources.supports: In 2021 the distributor reported 20 electrical incidents in the public domain to ESA, from contractors and homeowners contacting overhead or underground lines; none was a serious electrical incident (index 0 against a target of 0.049 per 1,000 km); it showed compliance through due diligence inspections, public safety concerns, compliance investigations and annual ESA audits, and the 2021 audit found it compliant in the five sections examined; its safety partners made 32 site visits to third-party contractors on limits of approach; public safety awareness index 72 percent.

assumptions: One file covers three kinds of item that share intake and closing: contact incident reports (about 62 percent), ESA findings, public safety concerns and inspection-found hazards (about 35 percent) and the annual audit and declaration cycle (about 3 percent, about one a year).
Public contacts reach this process through the health and safety process, as in the organisation file; in practice the first call usually comes from the control room or a trouble crew.
Field supervisors and the vice-president take part although the organisation file's process map lists only the safety manager, safety advisor and standards engineer.
The repair of a hazard ESA finds is done by crews in the maintenance and construction processes; this workflow counts only the supervisor's verification and follow-up.
Public awareness work (Component A of the scorecard: campaigns, contractor outreach, the awareness survey) is outside this workflow except the letter or visit after a contact.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's (wage x 1.40). External auditor fees and ESA time are not in labour cost.

The stated FTE (about 0.4) is about twice what step hands-on time times volume implies (about 0.2), because the roles also keep the compliance register, liaise with ESA by phone, reconcile scorecard data and maintain the construction verification program between items; none of that is written as a step.

Simulated median cycle time (about 20 days) matches the author's benchmark. By item type the simulation gives incident reports a median of about 17 days, ESA findings about 35 days and the audit cycle about 79 days from engaging the auditor to ESA's review meeting.
